steps.body: Degrees are a human invention — 360 slices because ancient astronomers liked the number. The circle offers its own unit: bend one RADIUS along the rim, and the angle it spans is **one radian**. Since the full rim is 2π radii long, a full turn holds 2π ≈ 6.28 radians.

widget.prompt: How many radians make one full circle? (Round to hundredths.)

commonErrors.feedback: 360 is the DEGREE count. In radians a full turn is the number of radius-lengths around the rim: 2π ≈ 6.28.
π ≈ 3.14 is only HALF the turn — the rim of a full circle is 2πr, so 2π radians.

explanationVariants: A quarter turn is a quarter of 2π: π/2 ≈ 1.57 radians.
Half of the half-turn π ≈ 3.14 gives 1.57.

widget.prompt: How many radians in a QUARTER turn (90°)? (Round to hundredths.)

commonErrors.feedback: 90 is the degree measure — radians count radius-lengths of arc: π/2 ≈ 1.57.
3.14 is π, the HALF turn (180°). A quarter turn is half of that: ≈ 1.57.

steps.body: Why bother? Because radians are the circle's NATIVE unit: they're a pure ratio (arc length ÷ radius), no unit attached — and every clean circle formula, starting with arc length s = rθ next lesson, works **only** when θ is in radians. Degrees always need converting first.

widget.prompt: One radian is about 57.3°. What makes it exactly that size?

options.label: It's the angle whose arc equals one radius — and 360° ÷ 2π ≈ 57.3
options.feedback: Right — geometry forces it: the full 360° splits among the 2π radius-arcs that wrap the rim.

options.label: It's exactly 60°
options.feedback: Close but no — 2π ≈ 6.28 arcs fit around, not exactly 6, so each is slightly UNDER 60°.

options.label: 57.3 is an arbitrary convention someone chose
options.feedback: Nothing arbitrary about it — once “arc = radius” defines the unit, 360/2π is forced by the circle itself.

options.label: It comes from splitting the circle into 100 parts
options.feedback: That's the gradian system (400 per turn). The radian comes from radius-lengths of arc, giving 2π per turn.

explanationVariants: Radians COUNT radius-lengths: an arc of 3 radii spans exactly 3 radians.
That's the whole beauty of the unit — no conversion, the arc count IS the angle.

widget.prompt: An arc along a circle's rim measures exactly 3 radius-lengths. What central angle does it span, in RADIANS?

commonErrors.feedback: 171.9° is the DEGREE conversion — the question asks for radians, where the radius-count is the answer: 3.
9.42 is 3π — a π multiplied in from habit. The radian count IS the radius count: 3.

steps.body: Converting hinges on one anchor: **180° = π radians**. Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180. Radians to degrees: multiply by 180/π. Keep the anchor in view and the factor's direction is never in doubt — the 180 sits opposite the π.

commonErrors.feedback: 1.57 is π/2 — that's 90°'s value, one anchor-notch too high. 60° = π/3 ≈ 1.05.

explanationVariants: 2 · 180/π ≈ 114.6° — two radians is about two 57.3° chunks.
Radians to degrees multiplies by 180/π, the anchor flipped.

widget.prompt: Convert 2 radians to degrees. (Round to tenths.)

commonErrors.feedback: 0.03 is 2 · π/180 — the factor ran the WRONG direction. Radians to degrees uses 180/π: ≈ 114.6°.
90° would make 2 radians a quarter turn — but one radian is already ≈ 57.3°, so two of them pass 114°.

hints: Each radian is about 57.3° — estimate first: two of them land near 115°.
The exact factor is 180/π (degrees on top, since degrees are wanted).

takeaways: One radian = the angle whose arc is one radius; 2π of them fill a turn.
Radians are a pure arc÷radius ratio — the unit circle formulas demand them.
Anchor 180° = π; the conversion factor points 180 at the unit you want.
steps.teaser: Next: fluency with the π-fraction angles you'll meet everywhere.

concept.body: One conversion, slowly. 90° is HALF of the anchor 180° = π, so 90° = π/2 ≈ 1.57 radians. Every conversion is just this: locate the angle as a fraction of 180, and attach that fraction to π.

explanationVariants: 90 is half of 180, so the radian measure is half of π.

commonErrors.feedback: 90 is still in degrees — the conversion to radius-counting hasn't happened: π/2 ≈ 1.57.
3.14 is the FULL anchor π = 180°. Ninety degrees is half of it: ≈ 1.57.
